articles.body: Exploration & Production October 16, 2026 · 1 minute ago More oil found at permit offshore Gabon NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Panoro Energy UK-headquartered Panoro Energy and Oslo-listed BW Energy have encountered more oil at a permit offshore Gabon by drilling two open-water wells. Panoro Energy reported on October 15 the conclusion of drilling two open-water wells to appraise the North-West Hibiscus area at the Dussafu Marin Permit offshore Gabon. Based on preliminary assessment, this represents an aggregate estimate of recoverable oil of approximately 8-9 million barrels. Dussafu is operated by BW Energy Gabon and Panoro’s interest in the license is 17.5%. The permit consists of multiple oil fields, including Moubenga, Walt Whitman, Ruche, Ruche North East, Tortue, Hibiscus and Hibiscus North. The latter five fields were discovered by Panoro and JV partners. According to the firm, the first well encountered a 16-meter oil column in high-quality Gamba reservoir sands adjacent to the Hibiscus field, while the second well, drilled as a side-track from the main well bore, confirmed the extension of the Hibiscus structure with the presence of a 30-meter oil column in high-quality Gamba sands within an as-yet undeveloped area of the Hibiscus field. The Borr Prospector 5 jack-up drilling rig is now mobilizing to the MaBoMo production platform, from where it will soon begin the planned MaBoMo Phase 2 drilling campaign, consisting of four new production infill wells in the Hibiscus and Hibiscus South fields. The first well is expected to come on stream in early 2027. As a result of the successful appraisal wells, the partners are assessing the addition of a fifth new production well at the end of the MaBoMo Phase 2 drilling campaign in the Hibiscus field. It is expected to drain an additional volume of at least 6 mmbls of oil. “The two latest successful appraisal wells further demonstrate the quality of the Hibiscus area and the substantial organic upside that remains within the Dussafu block," said Eric d’Argentré , Chief Operating Officer and President at Panoro Energy. "By leveraging the existing MaBoMo infrastructure, we are able to move quickly from subsurface success to development, with the addition of a fifth well to the Phase 2 campaign which will take gross Dussafu production back to nameplate capacity of 40,000 bopd.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
articles.summary: The SMAP mechanism introduced under the ETS represents an opportunity to help the maritime sector to transition towards clean fuels and propulsion technologies, and strengthen Europe’s industrial leadership. With an estimated support of €15 billion between 2028 and 2040, such a mechanism could encourage shipping...
articles.body: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 The SMAP mechanism introduced under the ETS represents an opportunity to help the maritime sector to transition towards clean fuels and propulsion technologies, and strengthen Europe’s industrial leadership. With an estimated support of €15 billion between 2028 and 2040, such a mechanism could encourage shipping companies to use green e-fuels, which will need to be scaled up in this period to meet long-term decarbonisation targets. The European Commission’s Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) mentions that in less than a decade, 4.6 million tonnes of e-fuels could be needed to reach FuelEU targets. A high price difference coverage in favour of e-fuels compared to other alternative fuels under SMAP is a welcome step, but is unlikely to be sufficient in itself to ensure a genuine move towards e-fuels. Because of the capital-intensive nature of e-fuels production, these projects will require producers to enter long-term offtake agreements with companies in order to secure investment. The current SMAP proposal is unlikely to provide sufficient support to this process. While some alternative fuels and zero-emissions propulsion technologies have a role to play in reducing maritime GHG emissions, SMAP should be used primarily to reward long-term e-fuel use, rather than short-term fuel and propulsion technological options which may already be incentivised under existing legislation. As negotiations on the ETS file continue, we encourage you to include following changes to SMAP to ensure the mechanism drives investments in genuine long-term e-fuel options: • 1 Earmark a significant portion of the SMAP allowances to e-fuels: This would ensure that the SMAP mechanism is used to assist long-term decarbonisation e-fuel options, including some produced in Europe, and does not only subsidise short-term solutions already available on the market. • 2 Include a book-in-advance mechanism applicable to e-fuels: In the absence of guaranteed price support, shipping companies are unlikely to sign long-term offtake agreements with e-fuel producers. A book-in-advance mechanism would improve the bankability of e-fuels projects, the vast majority of which remain at pre-FID stage. Such a mechanism has already been introduced under the SAF Allowance proposal. Source: European Federation for Transport and Environment 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Dry bulk safety: scrap metal fires, fumigation and enclosed spaces
articles.summary: BIMCO’s Dry Bulk Cargo Network discussed three persistent safety challenges at its latest meeting: fire risks from contaminated scrap metal cargoes, the shift of fumigation duties from specialists to ships’ crews, and continuing fatalities in enclosed spaces. Members highlighted the need for clearer cargo...
articles.body: Dry bulk safety: scrap metal fires, fumigation and enclosed spaces in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 BIMCO’s Dry Bulk Cargo Network discussed three persistent safety challenges at its latest meeting: fire risks from contaminated scrap metal cargoes, the shift of fumigation duties from specialists to ships’ crews, and continuing fatalities in enclosed spaces. Members highlighted the need for clearer cargo information, stronger charter party provisions, and practical measures to protect crews. The eighth meeting of the BIMCO Dry Bulk Cargo Network was held on Thursday 8 October 2026 and covered the following agenda items: Carriage of scrap metals Fumigation Enclosed spaces Carriage of scrap metals Scrap metals had previously been discussed at the sixth meeting in early 2025, when views differed over whether the IMSBC Code schedule for scrap adequately covers the different types of scrap and the effects of contamination by materials such as plastics, tyres, and oils. Self-heating and oxidation can increase the risk of fire, particularly when scrap is moved from outdoors storage, where drainage and ventilation are possible, into a cargo hold, where compaction can restrict both. The sixth meeting acknowledged that the risk can be mitigated to some extent by: Better understanding the type of scrap metal being loaded Building trust and credibility between owners and charterers or shippers Understanding the ports where issues are most likely to occur Improving charter party terms Checking P&I club guidance Engaging an independent cargo surveyor Avoiding Letters of Indemnity (LOIs), such as rain letters. However, this remains an issue, and BIMCO continues to receive member enquiries. These include questions about the meaning of “as dry as possible;” surveyors finding more plastics, tyres, oils and flammable material than the declared impurity percentage suggests; and the implications of lithium batteries being present, including whether this introduces dangerous goods considerations under Class 9 of the IMDG Code. Network members were asked: Are any changes needed to better address the risks associated with scrap cargoes? 13% said changes were required to charter parties only 13% said changes were required to the IMSBC Code Group C schedule only 65% felt changes were required to both charter parties and the Group C schedule 9% felt that the current arrangements were working well. Some members commented that the schedule itself is clear, but that problems arise at scrap yards and among shippers. These include confusion about the distinction between different scrap metal cargoes and how they should be described and classified, and a general lack of understanding of the hazards. Members also called for authorities to publish reports on fires related to the carriage of scrap metal. Members reported concerns about an apparent increase in fires related to the carriage of scrap cargoes but noted that the lack of formal investigation reports makes it difficult for the industry to identify causes and develop effective solutions. Any changes to the Group C schedule should address what materials may be mixed into scrap cargoes, whether the sorting and removal of unwanted materials is adequate, whether loading practices create additional risks, and how to ensure that the master receives the necessary information. Fumigation During the COVID-19 pandemic, travel and boarding restrictions sometimes prevented specialist fumigation contractors from sailing with vessels or boarding ships in port. As a result, some crews were asked to undertake activities normally carried out by specialists, including top-up fumigation and the removal of spent fumigant. This raised significant safety concerns, as IMO guidance generally envisages fumigants being handled only by qualified operators, and several serious accidents and fatalities have been linked to fumigation activities. The Thorco Angela casualty is a documented example in which investigators concluded that COVID-19 restrictions likely prevented specialist fumigators from boarding and that the crew were not trained to deploy or remove the fumigant. Several other accidents and fatalities were documented during the pandemic. In one recent casualty review, symptoms were initially attributed to COVID-19 rather than phosphine exposure, delaying identification of the actual hazard. Network members were asked whether, since the pandemic, they had observed operational responsibility for fumigated cargoes shifting from specialist service providers to ships’ crews. Of those able to answer: 25% had seen no change 42% had seen some or a significant shift of responsibility to the crew Only two members had seen less responsibility placed on the crew. Members were then asked which aspects of fumigation risk management are most commonly left to the ship’s crew after departure: 44%: gas monitoring 13%: training and awareness 21%: inspection of accommodation integrity 19%: response to exposure incidents. Other issues raised included obtaining a gas-free certificate, which can be difficult or impossible in some ports, and the safe disposal of fumigant sleeves by the crew. In what was seen as a positive development, none of the network members present had encountered a flag State still approving ships’ crews to undertake fumigation activities in place of specialist contractors. Enclosed spaces As time was short, the network held only a brief discussion on enclosed spaces to identify key topics for a future meeting. These include reading gas-detection meters, interpreting the results, and best practice for training and drills. Members noted that, despite greater awareness of enclosed-space risks and improved ability to assess atmospheres, accident and fatality statistics do not appear to be improving. Source: BIMCO 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Hong Kong Cements Its Position as a Resilient Global Maritime Hub Ahead of 10th Maritime Week
articles.summary: Hong Kong is preparing to host the 10th-anniversary edition of Hong Kong Maritime Week (HKMW 2026), taking place from November 15 to 21. articles.body: Hong Kong Cements Its Position as a Resilient Global Maritime Hub Ahead of 10th Maritime Week in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 Hong Kong is preparing to host the 10th-anniversary edition of Hong Kong Maritime Week (HKMW 2026), taking place from November 15 to 21. This year’s programme will bring together maritime professionals from around the world to discuss developments affecting global shipping, including changes in trade patterns, geopolitical uncertainty, decarbonisation, alternative fuels and ship finance. A “Safe Harbour” and “Super Connector” in Volatile Markets Hong Kong continues to position itself as a key maritime and financial centre in Asia, supported by its role under the “One Country, Two Systems” framework and its common law system. As the only common law jurisdiction within China, Hong Kong provides a legal and financial environment that supports the free flow of capital, data and talent, offering shipowners and institutional investors a degree of protection against market disruptions. The number of ship lessors operating in the city increased from 11 in 2020 to 64 in 2024, supported by government tax measures and deep capital markets capable of funding marine insurance and green technology projects. On the dispute resolution front, Hong Kong recorded a 56% surge in maritime arbitration cases in 2025. It is currently one of only four designated arbitration venues under the Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO) standard contracts and serves as the primary seat for PRC-related disputes. Operationally, Hong Kong is also expanding its green maritime fuel bunkering and trading hub. For operators facing conventional fuel price volatility, this hub aims to provide cost-effective, practical options for complying with international decarbonisation rules. Programme Highlights The week officially kicks off on November 16 with a hybrid Opening Ceremony at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre. The 45-minute session will feature keynote addresses from top policymakers and global industry leaders. On November 16 and 17, the World Maritime Merchants Forum will bring together industry experts to address geopolitical developments, trade disruption and sustainable shipping practices. The Asian Logistics, Maritime and Aviation Conference (ALMAC) will also take place on November 16 and 17, focusing on developments and opportunities across the region’s supply chains. On November 17, the conference will include a dedicated Belt and Road shipping seminar that spotlights Hong Kong’s status as a global shipping and investment hub, exploring new opportunities in infrastructure, technological innovation, and the green transition. On November 16, the International Chamber of Shipping will host the third Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit. Discussions will focus on supply chain resilience, maritime security and freedom of navigation. On November 17, the Hong Kong Maritime and Port Development Board will hold its second annual Flagship Summit under the theme “Capital Meets Cargo: Financing the Future of Global Trade”. The programme will cover ship finance, marine insurance and commodity markets. Following the Flagship Summit, HKMPDB will partner with the Financial Times to host an exclusive Dialogue Reception in the early evening, bringing togerher prominent guests from the maritime and financial sectors to exchange views in an intimate setting. The programme will also explore technical and technological developments across the industry. BIMCO will make its HKMW debut on November 18. In collaboration with the International Organization for Mediation, BIMCO will present a technical seminar on contractual developments related to the energy transition and maritime decarbonisation. On November 19, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) will host the half-day forum titled “Fueling Now and the Future: IBIA Hong Kong Forum on Alternative Marine Fuels”. The forum will cover the commercial adoption of alternative fuels, safety requirements, and supply chain readiness. To date, over 80 international organisations have confirmed plans to host around 60 events during HKMW 2026. For more information, please visit the HKMW 2026 event calendar. Source: Hong Kong Maritime Week 2026 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Vitol to launch Asian LNG bunkering in late 2026 in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 Marine fuel supplier Vitol Bunkers plans to start physical LNG bunker deliveries in Singapore and other Asian markets later this year. The announcement follows the completion of sea trials for its 12,500-cbm LNG bunkering vessel, Vivit Asia LNG. Vitol Bunkers said the planned operations are “backed by a fully contracted regional supply chain”. It also has another three LNG bunkering vessels on order, scheduled for delivery towards 2027. These will add a combined capacity of more than 50,000-cbm to its fleet. It has not specified which other Asian ports it plans to serve or when its first LNG bunker delivery will take place. “With long term LNG supply arrangements and bio-LNG production capability, customers benefit from the scale, reach and delivery capability needed to support requirements across key marine markets,” Vitol said. articles.title: DP World completes £13 million training hub at London Gateway
articles.summary: DP World and Thames Freeport have completed a new £13 million training and innovation centre at London Gateway in the United Kingdom. articles.body: DP World and Thames Freeport have completed a new £13 million training and innovation centre at London Gateway in the United Kingdom. The facility, known as The Hive, is located within London Gateway Logistics Park. It will support skills development in the maritime and logistics sectors, with plans to train around 1,125 people each year. The project was jointly funded by DP World and Thames Freeport. It aims to help businesses find skilled workers as London Gateway continues to expand. New training facilities for port and logistics workers The Hive includes a training centre equipped with crane operation simulators, virtual reality (VR) technology and facilities for working-at-height training. It will offer more than 100 days of industrial and employment training programmes each year. These programmes will help people develop skills for jobs in ports, logistics and related industries. The three-storey building also includes meeting rooms, an events area and a 100-seat auditorium. Other facilities include a gym and outdoor sports areas for employees working at the port and logistics park. “As the London Gateway Logistics Hub continues to grow, we want to ensure the infrastructure around it grows too,” said Alan Holland, Chief Executive Officer of DP World London Gateway Logistics Park. According to DP World, London Gateway supports more than 10,000 jobs through direct employment and its wider economic activities. Supporting the growth of London Gateway Construction of The Hive began in October 2025. The building has achieved BREEAM Outstanding certification and an EPC A+ energy rating. Training providers and other partners are expected to begin operating from the facility in November 2026. SEATS, which was appointed as the project’s skills partner earlier this year, will work with DP World and local employers to develop training programmes. The new centre forms part of wider efforts to support the growth of London Gateway and strengthen the local workforce.

articles.body: GT Wings expands product range with launch of new lightweight AirWing™S to reduce emissions for smaller vessels in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 GT Wings has announced the latest addition to its windassisted propulsion product range, AirWing™S, a new compact and lightweight Jet Sail developed to address the operational requirements of smaller commercial vessels. The new design expands the AirWing™ product line to address a broader segment of the commercial shipping market. With a streamlined lightweight configuration, the AirWing™S has been developed specifically for smaller vessels where vessel size, available deck space and weight considerations can influence the suitability of wind-assisted propulsion technology. The launch is the next step in GT Wings’ strategy to develop a scalable family of AirWing™ Jet Sails, enabling the technology to be adapted to differing requirements across the global commercial fleet. George Thompson, CEO of GT Wings, said: “The AirWing™S is an important addition to our product range. We know there is significant diversity across the global fleet, and wind propulsion solutions needs to reflect the different requirements of individual vessel types. By developing a compact AirWing™, specifically for smaller vessels, we can address another part of the market and make the emission reduction benefits of wind propulsion accessible to a wider range of shipowners.” New product launch alongside first commercial production The announcement comes as GT Wings marks a major milestone in the commercialization of its technology, with an Open House event showcasing the first customer-ordered AirWing™ units nearing completion at its partner Zunsion Technology’s manufacturing facility in Nantong. GT Wings announced a strategic manufacturing partnership with Zunsion Technology in March 2026. The partnership established a framework for industrial-scale production of AirWing™ systems in China, combining GT Wings’ wind propulsion and systems integration expertise with Zunsion’s manufacturing and assembly capabilities. The launch of the AirWing™S during the Open House event, alongside the first commercial AirWing™20 units, reflects GT Wings’ continued development of a scalable AirWing™ product family designed to meet the needs of a broader range of vessel types and operating requirements. Xu Jinbiao, CEO of Zunsion Technology, said: “It is a pleasure to welcome GT Wings, partners, and guests to Nantong and to showcase the progress being made here. The AirWing™ units now taking shape at our facility demonstrate what our partnership has already achieved, and we look forward to continuing to grow this partnership with GT Wings as its technology and product range continue to develop.” International collaboration in maritime innovation Open House attendees toured the facility and viewed two nearly completed 20m AirWing™ units ahead of delivery. The programme also included a keynote address by Ms. Marie Langrishe, Trade Counsellor for Technology and Industry, UK Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Technology of the UK Embassy to China in Beijing, as well as a technical update on the latest AirWing™ product developments. Ms. Langrishe commented: “GT Wings’ partnership with Zunsion highlights the value of combining UK innovation with global manufacturing expertise. It is encouraging to see a British-developed technology progressing towards international deployment, creating export opportunities and supporting sustainable growth. Collaborations like this help ensure that UK innovation can compete successfully on the world stage while contributing to the decarbonisation of the maritime sector.” The event brought together representatives from China, France, Hong Kong, Japan, Norway, the United Kingdom, and the wider international shipping industry, providing an opportunity to discuss the role of advanced manufacturing and maritime technology in supporting shipping’s transition towards lower-carbon operations. Guests toured the factory floor, viewed the two AirWing™20 units under construction, and heard directly from the GT Wings team about the continued development of its Jet Sail technology. George Thompson, GT Wings’ CEO, summarised: “Bringing together our customers, manufacturing partners, and representatives from around the world makes this an important moment for GT Wings. The AirWing™20 units taking shape in Nantong demonstrate our transition from technology development into repeatable commercial production. At the same time, we are continuing to expand the AirWing product family so that wind propulsion can deliver benefits across an increasingly broad range of vessel types and operating requirements.” Source: GT Wings 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
articles.summary: A Korean-developed integrated design framework has been developed to comprehensively analyze “ship survivability”—a naval vessel’s ability to avoid enemy attack, withstand damage when hit, restore key functions after damage, and continue its mission. The key achievement is the integration of survivability analyses...
articles.body: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework in International Shipping News 16/10/2026 A Korean-developed integrated design framework has been developed to comprehensively analyze “ship survivability”—a naval vessel’s ability to avoid enemy attack, withstand damage when hit, restore key functions after damage, and continue its mission. The key achievement is the integration of survivability analyses that had previously been performed using separate software tools into a single software environment. The AX Convergence Research Center of the Virtual Engineering Platform Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM, President Seog-Hyeon Ryu) developed ‘isSAFE,’ an integrated ship survivability design framework. isSAFE provides an integrated design environment in which a ship model can be built, various weapon hit scenarios can be generated, and vulnerability, recoverability, and results analyses can be performed in a continuous workflow. Ship survivability consists of three elements: susceptibility, the ability to avoid enemy detection and attack; vulnerability, the ability to withstand damage when hit; and recoverability, the ability to restore key functions after damage. Traditionally, each element has been analyzed using separate tools and procedures, with a significant reliance on foreign software. isSAFE generates a range of hit scenarios based on omnidirectional uniform distributions, probability-based distributions, and radar cross section (RCS) and infrared (IR) signatures. It also supports simplified and detailed vulnerability analyses for surface ships, as well as simplified analyses for underwater threats, allowing users to assess the extent of ship damage under different hit conditions. Dr. Euiyoung Kim, Principal Researcher at KIMM’s AX Convergence Research Center In particular, isSAFE can model a ship’s compartments, equipment, crew, and mission-essential systems such as propulsion, electrical power, and firefighting. It can then analyze damage under different threat and hit scenarios and assess whether key functions required for mission performance can be maintained. This enables users to compare survivability under different ship configurations and conditions and is expected to support the Republic of Korea Navy (ROK Navy), shipyards, and other end users in ship design and survivability assessments. The AX Convergence Research Center is continuing to enhance the damage-control-based recoverability analysis module and is developing integrated database management functions for reference information on threats, equipment, systems, and materials to broaden the scope of the framework. In subsequent development stages, the Center plans to enhance interoperability and extensibility with external analysis tools, develop software tailored to applications such as conceptual design and training, and expand collaboration with the ROK Navy, shipyards, and other end users. Operating screen of ‘isSAFE,’ KIMM’s integrated ship survivability design framework Dr. Euiyoung Kim, Principal Researcher at the AX Convergence Research Center, Virtual Engineering Platform Research Division, said, “The key feature of isSAFE is that it enables the three elements of ship survivability—susceptibility, vulnerability, and recoverability—to be addressed in an integrated manner within a single design framework.” She added, “We will continue to incorporate feedback from industry, academia, research institutes, and the military to further develop isSAFE into a framework that can be applied in ship design practice.” Dr. Euiyoung Kim, Principal Researcher at KIMM’s AX Convergence Research Center, reviews ship survivability analysis results using ‘isSAFE’ Meanwhile, the AX Convergence Research Center held the first public demonstration of isSAFE at 11:00 a.m. on October 8 at the main conference room in the R1 Building at KIMM’s Daejeon headquarters to present its key functions and gather feedback from participants. Using a virtual frigate-class warship model, the demonstration presented the major workflow—from modeling and hit scenario generation to vulnerability and recoverability analyses and results analysis—in real time. It also included hit analyses at attendee-designated locations and a comparison of analysis results from two models with the same hull but different propulsion configurations. The research was supported by KIMM’s institutional research program, “Development of core technologies for digital transformation to enhance the total life-cycle safety of next-generation special vessels,” which is currently in its third year. Source: Korea Institute of Machinery & Materials 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: The Shipping Ministry announced two specialised credit risk insurance products to support India’s shipbuilding industry under the National Shipbuilding Mission. articles.body: India: Shipping ministry unveils 2 specialised credit risk insurance products in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 16/10/2026 The Shipping Ministry announced two specialised credit risk insurance products to support India’s shipbuilding industry under the National Shipbuilding Mission. The Shipbuilding Project Credit Risk Insurance Policy (SbPCP), developed by ECGC Ltd, will cover export projects, while the Business Credit Shield Policy Shipbuilders (BCSPS), developed by The New India Assurance Co Ltd, will protect domestic projects, Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal announced at the concluding day of the 21st Maritime State Development Council (MSDC) held here. The central government will subsidise insurance premiums and provide direct support to insurers in case shipyards file claims, the minister said. Developed under the Shipbuilding Development Scheme (SbDS), these first-of-their-kind insurance policies aim to reduce financial stress in large-scale ship manufacturing. “Building a ship is a massive, multi-year journey, a single missed milestone payment could stall an entire shipyard’s operations. With these new insurance policies, we are stepping in to give them a real safety net. We want our shipyards to focus on what they do best, building world-class vessels, without the fear of delayed payments or sudden global market shifts holding them back,” said Sonowal. This was the first meeting of the MSDC after its recognition as a statutory consultative body under the Indian Ports Act, 2025, notified on May 15 this year. The Council, originally constituted in 1997, now functions with an enhanced mandate to promote integrated maritime growth, coordinated policy formulation, and planned development of maritime infrastructure. The Council endorsed the priorities of the National Perspective Plan and urged States to fast-track multimodal connectivity projects through road, rail, inland waterways, pipelines and conveyors. It resolved that States, in coordination with MoPSW, to develop port-linked industrial clusters with land availability, plug-and-play infrastructure and fast-tracked approvals, integrated with port capacity expansion and connectivity projects. Sonowal also launched the Ready Reckoner for Implementing ONOP, a comprehensive guide for major and other than major orts. The document includes references to central circularshissued by CBIC, Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for implementing inter-ministerial process reforms, and sets out clear expectations from state and Union Territory Governments to expedite ONOP implementation. “The MSDC has now entered a new statutory phase, strengthening cooperative federalism in maritime governance. With the adoption of MIV 2030 and MAKV 2047 targets, India’s ports and shipping sector will be future-ready, competitive and aligned with global standards. The Council’s resolutions today mark a decisive step towards integrated maritime growth and port-led industrialization,” Sonowal said. Source: PTI 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and Enterprise Singapore, through the Singapore Standards Council (SSC), launched a new Singapore Standard (SS) and two Technical References (TRs) today covering ammonia bunkering, bunker fuel sampling, and testing for polymers in residual based marine fuels....
articles.body: New Bunkering Standards Enhance Fuel Quality Assurance in Port News 16/10/2026 The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and Enterprise Singapore, through the Singapore Standards Council (SSC), launched a new Singapore Standard (SS) and two Technical References (TRs) today covering ammonia bunkering, bunker fuel sampling, and testing for polymers in residual based marine fuels. Announced at the Singapore International Bunkering Conference and Exhibition (SIBCON) 2026, the new standards will strengthen safety, consistency and fuel quality assurance for the bunkering industry as Singapore develops its capabilities for a multi-fuel future. Technical Reference (TR) 148:2026 – Advancing Ammonia Bunkering Operations 2. With ammonia emerging as one of the alternative marine fuels, TR 148:2026 Code of Practice for Ammonia Bunkering (TR 148) sets out the requirements for the safe and efficient conduct of ammonia bunkering operations. This includes custody transfer, bunkering procedures, safety and personnel competency. It provides a common framework for bunker suppliers, bunker craft operators, shipowners and other industry stakeholders to plan and conduct ammonia bunkering operations. Under the Singapore-Australia Green and Digital Shipping Corridor, MPA and the Pilbara Ports Authority will work together to validate TR 148 through the sharing of operational experience and relevant information from bunkering trials conducted at their respective ports. This collaboration will help build practical experience and strengthen the standards and operational requirements needed to support the safe and scalable deployment of ammonia bunkering globally. Singapore Standard (SS) 730:2026 – Strengthening Bunker Sampling of Ambient Liquid Marine Fuels SS 730:2026 Code of Practice for Bunker Sampling (SS 730) sets out requirements for custody transfer sampling of ambient liquid marine fuels, including Class F marine fuels, which are fuels made from petroleum, synthetic and renewable sources, and methanol. The Standard provides common sampling procedures and safety requirements for bunker suppliers, bunker craft operators, bunker buyers and bunker surveyors, strengthening consistency in bunker delivery and fuel quality assurance. Technical Reference (TR) 155:2026 – Enhancing Testing Standards for Polymers in Residual Based Marine Fuels TR 155:2026 Test Method for Polymers in Residual Based Marine Fuels (TR 155) establishes a common method for testing for polystyrene, polypropylene and polymethyl methacrylate in residual based marine fuels, including detection limits. This will improve consistency in how these polymers are identified and strengthen fuel quality assurance. Mr Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive, MPA, said, “As shipping transitions towards a wider range of marine fuels, our bunkering standards and capabilities must evolve with it. These new standards will support the industry’s transition and strengthen Singapore’s ability to serve the bunkering needs of global shipping as new fuel pathways develop.” Ms Choy Sauw Kook, Director-General (Quality & Excellence), Enterprise Singapore, said, “Standards are an important enabler of maritime decarbonisation, providing a common foundation for new fuels and practices to be adopted safely and consistently. As the marine fuel landscape evolves, TR 148, SS 730 and TR 155 extend this assurance across bunkering operations, fuel sampling and quality testing, including for emerging fuels such as ammonia. Together, they support Singapore’s transition to a multi-fuel future and reinforce our position as a trusted global bunkering hub.” Source: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: LNG, methanol and B24 bunkered at Ningbo-Zhoushan on same day in Port News 16/10/2026 This was the first time three different marine fuels had been supplied on the same day to different vessels berthed at the same port in China, according to the Ningbo Maritime Safety Administration (MSA). The LNG bunker vessel Haiyang Shiyou 302 delivered around 7,400 cbm (3,300 mt) of LNG at the Chuanshan port area on 30 September. The methanol bunker vessel Zhongran Green Energy 85 supplied around 7,500 mt of methanol at Meishan terminal, while Sijie 21 delivered around 3,000 mt of B24 biofuel blend at Daxie terminal. The report did not disclose the names of the receiving vessels or the fuel suppliers. The three bunkering operations marked the first time in China that three different marine fuels were supplied simultaneously to vessels berthed at the same port, according to the Ningbo MSA. “The ‘one port, three supplies’ model signifies a diversified and large-scale breakthrough” in the alternative fuel bunkering capacity of Ningbo-Zhoushan Port, Ningbo MSA added. Rise of methanol bunkering in China The methanol delivery also set a new record for the largest single methanol bunkering operation in Zhejiang province, the port authority said. Several Chinese ports have expanded their methanol bunkering activities over the past month. On 28 September, Sinobunker’s bunker vessel Daqing 268 supplied 300 mt of bio-methanol to COSCO’s container ship Carnation at the Nansha terminal in the Port of Guangzhou. The fuel was transferred via a ship-to-ship pipeline connection. The operation followed an earlier delivery by Daqing 268 of around 1,000 mt of pure bio-methanol to NYK Group’s dual-fuel bulk carrier Green Future at Guangzhou’s Lantau Anchorage. Bio-methanol in this operation was supplied by CIMC Enric. These two deliveries demonstrate Guangzhou Port’s ability to handle methanol bunkering at both terminals and anchorages, according to the port authority. Daqing 268 has also carried out methanol bunkering operations at terminals and anchorages in Shenzhen’s Yantian port area, Hong Kong and Ningbo. articles.title: China: Coal use reaching peak plateau amid green goals
articles.summary: China’s coal consumption is expected to enter a peak plateau transition during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), following a steady deceleration in growth as the country’s green energy transformation reshapes its economic fundamentals, said a think tank. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25), the...
articles.body: China: Coal use reaching peak plateau amid green goals in Commodity News 16/10/2026 China’s coal consumption is expected to enter a peak plateau transition during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), following a steady deceleration in growth as the country’s green energy transformation reshapes its economic fundamentals, said a think tank. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25), the country’s coal usage was characterized by rising total volume but a markedly slowing growth rate, according to the Report on China Energy Development 2026, released by the China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute in Beijing. In 2025, total coal consumption reached 4.76 billion metric tons, edging up a mere 0.1 percent year-on-year. Consequently, coal’s share in China’s primary energy consumption mix fell to 51.4 percent, a drop of 1.8 percentage points from the previous year. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, as China accelerates the construction of a new energy system, promotes the clean and efficient utilization of coal, upgrades traditional industries and replaces scattered coal — referring to coal of poor quality which is used throughout the civil sector for household cooking, heating and various commercial applications — national coal consumption will enter a peak plateau period, the report said. The institute said power generation — which accounts for roughly 63 percent of the nation’s coal usage — saw a 1.9 percent decline in coal-fired electricity generation in 2025, driving a 2 percent drop in thermal coal demand. The steel and building materials sectors — which account for about 15 percent and 6 percent of coal consumption, respectively — also registered declines. Crude steel production fell 4.4 percent, while cement and flat glass output dropped by 6.9 percent and 3 percent, respectively, leading to markedly lower coal burning in heavy industries, it said. In sharp contrast, the coal chemical sector remained robust. Driven by high operating loads at new coal chemical facilities and strong output of major chemical products, the sector’s coal demand surged more than 10 percent, outpacing its 2024 growth rate. The chemical sector currently represents about 9 percent of China’s total coal consumption. Coal-fired power in China is experiencing a major structural transition, shifting from a primary baseload energy source to a more flexible, supportive backup, said Liu Zhiqiang, deputy director of the China Electricity Council’s planning and development department. “Although coal plants are seeing fewer annual utilization hours to make way for renewable energy alternatives, their crucial role in maintaining grid stability — such as offering frequency support and rotational inertia — is increasingly vital,” Liu said. He cautioned that even though renewable capacity has reached historic highs, installed capacity does not necessarily equate to actual power output. As solar power fluctuates and operates for far fewer hours than fossil fuels due to its intermittent nature, Liu said coal will continue to serve as the critical “ballast stone” ensuring the reliable operation of the national grid for the near term. The institute said the absolute volume of coal consumed still grew over the past five years, with total coal consumption up from 4.05 billion tons to 4.76 billion tons. This underscores coal’s enduring yet transitional role in ensuring national energy security even as its share of the overall energy mix steadily declines. Source: China Daily 2026-10-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims
articles.summary: British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from...
articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Ports and Logistics Regulatory UK ports hit back at Brussels over ETS diversion claims Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 42 3 minutes read UK Government UK Government British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory linking rising UK container activity to the bloc’s Emissions Trading System, arguing that new capacity, changing liner networks and commercial competition offer more convincing explanations. In a new report, the association said around 85% of the UK’s container traffic growth in 2025 was concentrated in London, following the opening of DP World’s £350m ($465m) fourth berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Government figures show UK ports handled 11% more containers last year, equivalent to an additional 600,000 units. London accounted for roughly 500,000 of those, with its growth driven largely by the additional capacity at London Gateway. The DP World terminal handled more than 3m teu in 2025, up 52% from 1.9m teu a year earlier. The increase followed the opening of the fourth berth, which boosted capacity by more than a third, and the arrival of Asia-Europe services operated by Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd’s Gemini Cooperation in February 2025. London Gateway has been challenging Felixstowe’s position as Britain’s busiest boxport, with Maersk’s departure from the Hutchison-operated facility reshaping the country’s container market. DP World is pressing ahead with another £1bn ($1.33bn) expansion, adding two all-electric berths and a second rail terminal. The BPA argues that such investment and network changes have been overlooked in assessments linking Britain’s expanding container business to EU carbon pricing. The dispute follows research by Spain’s Puertos del Estado, which found the UK’s share of northern European deepsea shipping activity, measured in teu-miles, rose from 17.5% in 2023 to 32.1% by July 2025. Subsequent analysis put the figure at around 36% in the first quarter of 2026, broadly mirroring declines in Germany and the Netherlands. The Spanish study also estimated that 76% of observed route changes were attributable to the EU ETS, raising concerns that containerlines were restructuring their networks to reduce carbon costs. But the BPA has questioned both the methodology and the conclusions. It argues that teu-miles, which combine vessel capacity with voyage distance, measure shipping network activity rather than actual containers handled. The metric can also be distorted by longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope and changes to the sequence of port calls. The association also disputes treating the widely cited 76% figure as evidence of carbon-driven diversion specifically to Britain, arguing that the available analysis does not isolate the effects of ETS from alliance restructuring, congestion and new terminal capacity. Continental European ports have not uniformly lost ground either. Rotterdam’s container throughput increased 3.1% to 14.2m teu in 2025, Hamburg recorded 7.3% growth to 8.3m teu, while Antwerp-Bruges posted a 0.7% increase. The disagreement comes after the European Commission proposed tightening rules designed to prevent containerships from using neighbouring non-EU ports to reduce their ETS exposure. Under proposals unveiled in July, certain container ports within 150 nautical miles of an EU port could be excluded from the definition of a port of call for emissions accounting purposes. The threshold for transhipment activity at other qualifying non-EU ports within 300 nautical miles would also be lowered from 65% to 50%. The changes could bring more British terminals within the EU’s anti-evasion framework, potentially increasing carbon costs for shipping lines using them. The proposals have yet to be adopted. “It would be extraordinary if the EU responded to that success by introducing new measures to penalise British ports,” said Mark Simmonds, the BPA’s director of policy and external affairs. The association stressed that it supports shipping decarbonisation but warned against treating normal competition between ports as regulatory avoidance. Britain has already brought domestic shipping and emissions in UK ports into its own emissions trading scheme from July this year, while plans to extend carbon pricing to international voyages from 2028 are also under consideration. The BPA has urged the UK government and the European Commission to reassess the evidence before proceeding with measures that could affect port competitiveness and future investment on both sides of the Channel. articles.body: Stena Line has reached an agreement to acquire the RoRo vessel Somerset from CLdN as part of a broader restructuring of its freight network. Subject to completion and transfer, the vessel is expected to join Stena Line’s Dublin–Liverpool service in early December. Delivery of Somerset is expected later in October. The vessel will then enter dry dock for refurbishment and repainting before being renamed Stena Freighter. Somerset previously operated within Stena Line’s network as a chartered vessel. Dublin–Liverpool service returns to one vessel Stena Line currently operates the Rotterdam–Harwich route with two chartered vessels: Mistral, owned by Godby Shipping, and Thuleland, owned by Wallenius SOL. The charter agreements are due to expire, and both ships will be returned to their owners at the end of the year. Stena Scotia and Stena Hibernia will subsequently be redeployed from the Dublin–Liverpool route to Rotterdam–Harwich. The North Sea connection will continue to operate with two vessels, both owned by Stena Line. Stena Freighter will replace Stena Scotia and Stena Hibernia on Dublin–Liverpool. As a result, the Irish Sea freight route will return to a single-vessel operation after being served by two ships for most of 2026. “We are very pleased with the agreement to acquire Somerset. It’s a vessel that fits well within our network and has the flexibility and capacity to operate on several of our routes,” said Magnus Lander, Head of Network & Business Development at Stena Line. “We know Somerset well from her previous service with us and know what she can deliver. With Somerset, we have an excellent option with significant capacity for the Dublin–Liverpool route,” he added. Lander said the acquisition would also allow Stena Line to strengthen its position on the Rotterdam–Harwich route by deploying Stena Scotia and Stena Hibernia. Built by Flender Werft in Germany in 1999, Somerset measures 183.4 metres in length and offers 2,504 lane metres of freight capacity.

articles.title: International Seaways seals $370m Bruton takeover deal

The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the Lois Zabrocky-led group acquire Bruton’s entire four-ship supertanker portfolio, going...
articles.body: Americas Europe Tankers International Seaways seals $370m Bruton takeover deal Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 415 3 minutes read Bruton Bruton New York-listed tanker owner International Seaways has struck a deal to take over Tor Olav Trøim-backed Bruton in a transaction valuing the Oslo-listed VLCC company at around $370m. The agreement, announced on Friday, will see the Lois Zabrocky-led group acquire Bruton’s entire four-ship supertanker portfolio, going considerably further than the sale of two newbuildings first linked to the US owner in market reports last week. International Seaways has secured agreements with shareholders representing 50.5% of Bruton, including Trøim’s Drew Holdings and Koch Inc, to exchange their holdings for newly issued shares in the US company. The exchange is set at 0.0519 International Seaways shares for each Bruton share, with the initial transaction expected to settle around October 20. The remaining shares will be acquired through a merger, with Seaways expecting to issue approximately 3.12m new shares, accounting for 96% of the total consideration. Smaller Bruton shareholders will receive cash at $6.3044 per share. The deal brings four 300,000 dwt VLCCs into the Seaways fold, including the LNG dual-fuel Mount Vision , which entered service in July, and sistership Mount Horizon , scheduled for delivery from China’s New Times Shipbuilding next month. The remaining two vessels, Mount Frontier and Mount Summit , are due in August and October 2027. The first two ships already have substantial charter cover. Mount Vision secured a 3+1+1-year arrangement with a trading house, earning $95,000 per day for the initial nine months before switching to an index-linked structure. Mount Horizon has been fixed for 12 to 15 months at $105,700 per day. The two 2027 newbuildings remain unchartered and have been at the centre of the recent sale speculation. Splash detailed the potential deal last week after Bruton acknowledged market rumours and launched a strategic review. At the time, International Seaways was linked to the purchase of at least two newbuildings, with brokers discussing values north of $200m per vessel. Bruton’s own figures put the original yard cost of the two 2027 ships at about $117m apiece, highlighting how sharply modern VLCC asset values have moved. The $370m announced on Friday, however, represents the valuation of Bruton’s equity rather than the gross value of its vessels. The takeover follows a major restructuring of Trøim’s tanker interests. Bruton originally built up a 12-ship VLCC programme before splitting the business in August, retaining its first four New Times ships and transferring another eight newbuildings into separately listed OMC Tankers. The demerger left Bruton with a concentrated fleet of near-term deliveries, substantial charter cover and financing arrangements with Chinese lessors covering 85% to 90% of construction costs. The eight vessels in OMC Tankers are not part of the International Seaways transaction. For International Seaways, the acquisition continues an aggressive fleet renewal programme that has seen the company dispose of older tonnage while selectively investing in younger ships. The US owner had a fleet of around 70 vessels, including newbuildings, before the deal. It sold seven older tankers, including two VLCCs, earlier this year for more than $216m and has also invested in LR1 newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding. The company strengthened its crude tanker trading platform in January by taking full ownership of Tankers International, which subsequently expanded into the suezmax market. The latest acquisition comes against an exceptionally strong earnings backdrop. Alongside the takeover announcement, International Seaways unveiled preliminary third-quarter net income of $340m to $350m, including a roughly $50m gain from the sale of a suezmax. It reported liquidity of approximately $965m at the end of September. The transaction also brings together businesses associated with two familiar names in Norwegian shipping. Family trusts established by John Fredriksen, Trøim’s former longtime business partner, hold a 13.54% stake in International Seaways, according to the latest US regulatory filing. The pair went their separate ways in 2014 after nearly two decades working together. Bruton’s board has unanimously recommended the transaction, with a shareholder vote expected around October 30. Completion is targeted for early November, subject to the necessary approvals, after which Bruton intends to delist from Euronext Growth Oslo. articles.title: Lower emissions do not always signal a more efficient container voyage
articles.summary: Lower total emissions do not necessarily mean that a container ship voyage operated more efficiently, according to a new VesselBot case study examining the relationship between emissions and transported cargo. The analysis compares two voyages performed by the same vessel between Bremerhaven and Norfolk in May and...
articles.body: Lower total emissions do not necessarily mean that a container ship voyage operated more efficiently, according to a new VesselBot case study examining the relationship between emissions and transported cargo. The analysis compares two voyages performed by the same vessel between Bremerhaven and Norfolk in May and July 2026. The May voyage generated 3,104 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent emissions while carrying 2,783 TEUs. This resulted in emissions of 1.12 tonnes of CO₂e per TEU. By comparison, the July voyage produced 2,547 tonnes of CO₂e and transported 2,077 TEUs. Although its total emissions were 557 tonnes lower, its emissions intensity reached 1.23 tonnes of CO₂e per TEU. Consequently, the voyage with the higher absolute emissions transported its cargo more efficiently when emissions were measured against the volume carried. Cargo utilisation shapes voyage emissions efficiency VesselBot said that total CO₂e measures the environmental impact of a voyage but does not indicate how efficiently those emissions were used to transport cargo. To assess voyage emissions efficiency, the company uses Well-to-Wake emissions intensity, measured in grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre. The metric relates emissions to the amount of cargo transported and the distance over which it was carried. According to the case study, the average Well-to-Wake emissions intensity across container ship voyages during the second quarter of 2026 was 231.7 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre. Average emissions amounted to 651.3 tonnes of CO₂e per voyage. VesselBot divided the voyages into six emissions-intensity categories. Voyages in the most efficient category, producing up to 49 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre, generated an average of 1,511 tonnes of CO₂e per voyage. In contrast, voyages in the least efficient category, producing at least 800 grams of CO₂e per TEU-kilometre, emitted an average of 545 tonnes. The most efficient voyages recorded average vessel utilisation of 80% and transported 8,946 TEUs. Average utilisation in the least efficient category fell to 31%, with only 340 TEUs carried. The findings indicate that highly utilised vessels can generate more emissions in absolute terms while distributing those emissions across considerably more transport work. Voyage-level modelling supports accurate comparisons VesselBot noted that emissions-intensity calculations depend on the accuracy of the underlying voyage emissions estimates. Fuel consumption is influenced by vessel characteristics, engine performance, sailing speed, time at sea, port stays and operating conditions. As a result, comparisons based only on voyage distance or general industry averages may not accurately represent individual vessel operations. Combining fuel-consumption modelling with shipment-level cargo data allows emissions to be compared with the transport work delivered by each voyage. According to VesselBot, this approach can help shippers evaluate carriers, services and individual sailings on a more comparable basis. It can also distinguish between a voyage that produces fewer emissions because it transports less cargo and one that genuinely uses fuel more efficiently. The study concludes that absolute emissions and operational efficiency should be treated as separate measures when evaluating the environmental performance of container shipping.

UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. “West Africa looks set to remain the fastest growing long-haul source of dry bulk cargo,” Tradeviews stated. The growth is already evident. The five West African exporters covered by the consultancy shipped 160.1m tonnes in their principal trades during the first eight months of this year, up 25% year on year. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Bauxite exports, meanwhile, are forecast to retreat from a peak of nearly 194m tonnes this year to 153m tonnes by 2030 as Guinea pushes ahead with domestic alumina processing. A capesize round voyage between Guinea and China takes approximately 78 days, compared with just 29 days on the Australia-China route. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. There are, however, already signs that the region’s growth ambitions are running up against freight market realities. In its latest weekly report, BRS Shipbrokers noted that exceptionally high freight rates had priced some higher-cost Guinean bauxite miners out of the export market. Guinea shipped 15.61m tonnes of bauxite in September, down 12% from August, with freight costs at one point accounting for more than half the delivered value of the commodity. The subsequent easing in capesize rates could provide some relief. The C3 benchmark has fallen from $43.43 a tonne in late September to $32.95 on October 12, prompting BRS to suggest Guinean bauxite exports could recover by 5% to 10% month on month during November and December. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September. SSY has similarly warned that Guinean bauxite exports have retreated from early-September highs, observing that “shipping demand is turning more sensitive to margin levels on the mining side”. Tradeviews did also caution that potential Guinean bauxite export restrictions, Simandou project delays, dedicated ore carriers and the displacement of Australian iron ore shipments could reduce the benefits for the wider capesize market with much of the market increasingly looking like a Chinese conveyor belt. SSY noted in a market report from August that VLOCs of more than 220,000 dwt accounted for nearly half of Simandou shipments during the first half of 2026. More significant for independent owners is what is coming down the slipways. SSY data shows Chinese tonnage accounts for nearly 40% of the current VLOC orderbook, raising questions over how much of Simandou’s enormous prospective tonne-mile demand will ultimately filter through to the conventional capesize spot market. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.title: ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation
articles.summary: ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind...
articles.body: Subsea October 16, 2026 · 3 hours ago ScottishPower Renewables completes ‘record-breaking’ cable landfall operation 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email ScottishPower Renewables ScottishPower Renewables has completed what it says was a record-breaking cable landfall operation for its 960 MW East Anglia Two offshore wind farm in the UK, installing two nearly 1.8-kilometer-long ducts beneath the Suffolk coastline and seabed for the project’s export cables. The ducts, each measuring 800 millimeters in diameter, were installed using horizontal directional drilling (HDD), a technique that creates an underground passage without excavating beaches or disturbing the coastline directly. ScottishPower Renewables says the operation involved the world’s longest continuous single sections of extruded polyethylene (PE) ducts and represents the largest electricity transmission landfall of its kind in the UK, based on the combination of duct length and diameter. Manufactured by Pipelife in Norway, the ducts were produced as single uninterrupted lengths, eliminating the need for welded joints. They will provide a protected route for the high-voltage export cables carrying electricity from the offshore wind farm to shore. The landfall works form part of the project’s onshore civil engineering program, led by OCU Group with support from its subsidiary Peter McCormack & Sons. ScottishPower Renewables said the operation also marked a manufacturing record for Pipelife, whose ducts measured approximately 1,793 meters each. “The completion of this colossal HDD, which is three times the length of our other East Anglia projects, is a huge achievement – quite literally – and a major milestone as we progress construction of our third windfarm in the region,” said Ross Ovens , ScottishPower Renewables’ Managing Director for Offshore. “Landfall works are known to be one of the most technically challenging aspects of building an offshore windfarm, but thanks to precision planning and a great partnership with our principal contactor OCU Group and duct manufacturer Pipelife, this programme has well and truly hit the mark – breaking UK and world records in the process.” The milestone comes as East Anglia Two advances towards offshore construction, with the first export cable expected to be installed in summer 2027, and commercial operation targeted for late 2028. The 960 MW offshore wind farm will be built at a site in the southern North Sea, around 33 kilometers off the Suffolk coast at its nearest point, where 64 Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD wind turbines will be installed on monopile foundations. articles.title: ESPO and EFIP introduce green innovation platform for European ports
articles.summary: The European Sea Ports Organisation (ESPO) and the European Federation of Inland Ports (EFIP) have made the Green Innovation Compass available on their websites. The online platform helps maritime and inland ports find practical solutions for greener and more efficient operations. It brings together research, case...
articles.body: The European Sea Ports Organisation (ESPO) and the European Federation of Inland Ports (EFIP) have made the Green Innovation Compass available on their websites. The online platform helps maritime and inland ports find practical solutions for greener and more efficient operations. It brings together research, case studies and experience from port projects across Europe. The platform focuses on technologies that can help ports reduce emissions, improve efficiency and modernise their infrastructure. Helping ports choose new technologies The Green Innovation Compass was developed through MAGPIE, a European research project that brought together ports, companies, researchers and public authorities. The platform covers electrification, alternative fuels, automation, digitalisation and resilience. It explains how different technologies work, where ports can use them and what they need before introducing them. Ports can search for solutions based on their needs, priorities and project timelines. They can also explore examples from other European ports and learn from their experience. The aim is to make information on port innovation easier to find and use. Rather than recommending one solution for every port, the platform helps users compare different options. Encouraging cooperation between ports ESPO and EFIP want the platform to support greater cooperation across Europe’s port sector. Both organisations believe that sharing experience can help ports overcome common challenges. “The Green Innovation Compass allows for inland ports to see what projects others have already realised,” said Turi Fiorito, Director of EFIP. Isabelle Ryckbost, Secretary General of ESPO, also encouraged ports to use the platform and share their knowledge. The Green Innovation Compass will continue to expand as ports and other organisations contribute new projects and examples. The Alliance for Logistics Innovation through Collaboration in Europe (ALICE) will help maintain the platform after the MAGPIE project ends. The platform is available at GreenInnovationCompass.eu .

articles.body: ID Logistics has opened a new 35,000 sqm logistics centre in Germany, bringing its network in the country to 17 facilities. The site, located at Mittelweserpark in Lower Saxony, began operations in September 2026 and focuses on handling heavy and bulky goods. The opening marks another step in the company’s expansion in Germany. Since 2021, ID Logistics has more than doubled its network, growing from eight to 17 sites. Its German operations now cover 910,000 sqm of logistics space and employ 4,800 people, compared with 2,800 five years ago. New facility strengthens bulky goods operations The new centre consists of three buildings and can accommodate up to 7,000 oversized items weighing as much as 180 kg. It handles products such as household appliances, sofas and leisure equipment. Operations include order preparation, dispatch and cross-docking. According to ID Logistics, orders can be ready for dispatch within two hours of receipt, while cross-docking shipments have a maximum processing time of four hours. The company has invested in 40 material-handling vehicles, including equipment designed for large and heavy products. Once fully operational, the facility will employ 150 people. The opening also brings ID Logistics’ total space dedicated to heavy and bulky goods in Germany to more than 100,000 sqm. Expanding logistics services across Germany ID Logistics has operated in Germany since 2013. Its services cover warehousing, order preparation, sorting and last-mile delivery, which it introduced in 2024. The company is also developing its transport operations, including full truckload (FTL), less-than-truckload (LTL) and distribution services. The new facility builds on experience from the company’s existing 60,000 sqm centre in Göttingen, which has handled heavy and bulky goods since 2018. Before the Mittelweserpark site opened, some employees completed a three-week training programme in Göttingen to prepare for the new operations. The expansion strengthens ID Logistics’ position in the German contract logistics market, particularly in the handling and distribution of large consumer goods.

articles.title: GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck
articles.summary: Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. articles.body: Greater China Shipyards GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck Adis Ajdin October 16, 2026 0 56 2 minutes read GSI GSI Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a framework agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group, bringing the heavy-steel fabricator into its shipbuilding operations. GSI said its expanding orderbook and increasingly complex vessel mix would drive up demand for hull blocks over the coming years, prompting the move to bring in additional manufacturing capacity. Shanhaiguan, founded in 1894, specialises in bridge steel structures and railway equipment and operates six production bases across China. Under the agreement, it will allocate fabrication resources to ship blocks and take responsibility for production quality, safety and delivery schedules. Neither the contract value nor the volume of work has been disclosed. The agreement comes with GSI’s production schedule already stretching towards the end of the decade. The Guangzhou-based builder disclosed earlier this year that its contracted business was approaching RMB100bn ($14bn), with overseas orders accounting for more than 95% and construction slots extending into 2030. Its most recent intake includes 10 MR tankers ordered by Greek owner Evangelos Pistiolis’ Central Group, four additional MR vessels for Advantage Tankers and more LNG dual-fuel car carriers for MSC-controlled Global Car Carriers. GSI is also expanding its physical footprint. In May, it signed a joint venture agreement with Guangdong Port and Shipping Group to develop the 360,000 sq m Xiaohudao shipbuilding base in Guangzhou. A separate project launched in September will see a new facility built at Longxue North, with GSI lined up to operate the yard once completed in 2029. The latter is designed to produce up to 18 vessels annually. The Shanhaiguan deal is not an isolated move. Several Chinese bridge and structural-steel manufacturers have entered shipbuilding this year, taking on fabrication work previously handled by established yards. In June, China Railway Baoji Bridge Group’s Yangzhou subsidiary began manufacturing hull sections for a 73,000 dwt self-propelled deck carrier. The project involves 110 blocks across the vessel’s cargo section, with the largest weighing about 190 tonnes. Jingjiang Nanyang Shipbuilding is providing construction coordination, with China Classification Society overseeing technical and quality requirements. Another bridge specialist, Jingjiang Heavy Industry, followed in September, starting work on blocks for a 40,400 dwt bulk carrier. The China Railway Construction Corporation subsidiary is fabricating 10 cargo-hold bottom sections weighing up to 96 tonnes each, which are to be transported to Shanghai for final assembly. The company has established three outdoor block assembly lines and is targeting annual ship block production of up to 100,000 tonnes, with longer-term ambitions to move into complete vessel construction. Other Chinese shipbuilders have opted to expand fabrication capacity closer to home. Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding commissioned an expansion of its curved-block workshop in late 2025, adding nearly 23,000 sq m of production space. Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding also proposed a new block fabrication and assembly facility last year to address capacity constraints and reduce its reliance on external subcontractors. The moves form part of a broader capacity buildout across China. Broker BRS Group identified at least seven dormant shipyards being reactivated and a further dozen established facilities expanding production capacity, developments covered by Splash earlier this year. South Korean builders have been taking similar steps to overcome production bottlenecks. In April, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries introduced a split-hull construction method for a 157,000 dwt suezmax, outsourcing the 168 m bow section to HSG Sungdong Shipbuilding before joining it to a stern section built at Ulsan. HJ Shipbuilding & Construction has also shifted work outside its Yeongdo yard, contracting Daesun Shipbuilding in February to manufacture deckhouse blocks for eight 7,900 teu containerships after its own facilities reached capacity. articles.body: DHL Freight has introduced the SuperPanther eTopas 600 electric truck into regular commercial operations in the Netherlands. The vehicle also serves cross-border routes to Belgium, marking its move from testing to daily freight transport. The battery-electric heavy-duty truck has been operating since September 2026. It covers around 2,000 kilometers per week and offers a range of up to 500 kilometers on a single charge. Unlike vehicles assigned to fixed routes, the eTopas 600 operates across different parts of DHL Freight’s network. This allows the company to assess how electric trucks perform under changing transport requirements. From testing to commercial operations The deployment follows a series of trials carried out by DHL Freight and SuperPanther. The companies began working together in September 2024, before testing the vehicle in Austria earlier this year. During a two-week trial in spring 2026, the truck covered approximately 1,900 kilometers. The first European-built eTopas 600 was completed in July and entered commercial service two months later. According to DHL Freight, initial operating results have been positive, with the truck meeting its planned transport requirements. “Our experience from daily operations has been positive so far. The vehicle meets the requirements of the planned deployment profiles and achieves high productivity within the network,” said Arjan van Weelden, Carrier & Sustainability Manager at DHL Freight Netherlands. DHL plans further electric fleet expansion DHL Freight plans to add around 40 electric trucks to its fleet over the coming months. The company is using data from the eTopas 600 to assess how battery-electric vehicles can support regular freight operations, including international routes. “Our customers are looking for practical ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from their transport operations,” said Heidi van Eldik, CEO of DHL Freight Netherlands & Belgium. DHL Freight currently operates around 1,700 vehicles designed to reduce transport emissions. The company is also testing different vehicle technologies as part of DHL Group’s target to achieve net-zero emissions in logistics by 2050.
