articles.title: Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology
articles.summary: The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and...
articles.body: Contributions Tech Shipping’s AI winners will build capability, not buy technology Splash October 16, 2026 0 85 3 minutes read Gerd Altmann via Pixabay Gerd Altmann via Pixabay The technology is already widely available. The advantage will come from how shipping companies turn it into specialised systems, define its place in the team and manage adoption, says Michalis Gkontas, co-founder and CEO of AskChief. Today’s AI systems can already perform useful knowledge work. They can search and interpret large volumes of information, compare documents, prepare drafts and help people work through complex tasks. The more important question now is whether organisations are ready to deploy them well. Giving employees access to a general-purpose AI tool is easy. Turning that access into better technical work, stronger compliance and additional team capacity is a management challenge. Leaders must decide where AI should be used, what knowledge it can draw on and where professional responsibility remains. Access is not capability As connectivity improves across fleets, many seafarers can access the same general-purpose AI tools as colleagues ashore, whether or not their company has formally deployed them. A report or proposed response may arrive in polished language without showing what evidence supports it, which company procedure applies or how much was generated by AI. Fluent output is not necessarily useful output. Generic AI can make weak reasoning look convincing or produce material that does not fit the vessel’s actual circumstances. The shore team must then reconstruct the context and verify the basis of what it has received. A generic model does not naturally know which version of a company’s safety management system is current, whether a manual applies to the equipment fitted on a particular vessel or who must approve a proposed SMS change. Specialisation comes from the system built around the model: the company’s knowledge, role-specific instructions, specialist tools, established workflows, permissions and review points. The underlying model may be general-purpose. The operational system should not be. Begin with work that matters The weakest deployment brief is simply to “use AI more”. It leaves each employee to decide what the technology is for, which information is appropriate to use and how much confidence to place in the result. A stronger starting point is a recurring piece of work the team already understands: investigating a technical issue, preparing for an inspection, answering an SMS question or assessing how a new requirement affects company procedures. The task should be meaningful enough to matter but bounded enough to manage. Once the team sees AI supporting a familiar workflow, expansion becomes an operational decision rather than an abstract technology initiative. Let AI do the work around the decision AI is well suited to locating relevant material, assembling context, comparing records, identifying potential gaps and preparing a first draft. People remain responsible for interpreting the evidence, challenging its relevance, resolving uncertainty and approving the action. Its purpose is not to diminish professional expertise, but to extend its reach. A useful shorthand is the 10-80-10 rule. It is not a literal allocation of time or effort, but a sequence for organising the work. In the first 10%, the expert defines the problem, supplies the context and sets the standard for a good outcome. AI carries much of the middle 80% by finding information, structuring it, comparing records and preparing the work. In the final 10%, the accountable professional challenges the result, corrects it and decides what happens next. The percentages should change with the risk. A safety-critical decision may require far more human review than a routine summary. Make adoption a team practice Leaders need to set expectations, appoint owners and create simple feedback loops. Teams should be able to share useful cases, flag weak outputs, and show where information or workflow design needs improvement. In shipping, caution is usually rational. A confident but incorrect answer can waste time or introduce risk. Trust grows when users can inspect the underlying evidence, understand the system’s boundaries and see that their professional judgement remains central. The same discipline should shape measurement. Logins and prompts reveal little. Better questions are whether the team reached a reviewed outcome faster, used relevant company history, avoided duplicate work and captured the decision for the next person. Deployment will create the advantage AI models will keep becoming more powerful and widely available. Access will not be scarce, and it will not provide a durable advantage on its own. The difference will come from deployment: choosing the right work, building specialised systems around it and helping teams incorporate those systems into everyday operations. For leaders, this means treating AI neither as a standalone IT purchase nor as an instruction to reduce headcount. It is an opportunity to give capable people better tools and increase what the organisation can accomplish without weakening accountability. The technology exists. The management challenge is to turn it into a working organisational capability. The shipping companies that do this well will not simply have more people using AI. They will have better-equipped teams, stronger company knowledge and more capacity to act. articles.body: Fincantieri is accelerating the use of artificial intelligence and robotics across its shipyards through its BOOST² innovation programme. The initiative includes planned investments of nearly €100 million to improve shipbuilding efficiency, safety and production processes. The Italian shipbuilding group launched BOOST² – The Shipyard of the Future three years ago. Since then, more than 450 employees across 13 shipyards have taken part in the programme, including teams in Italy, Romania and the United States. Fincantieri presented its latest progress at the Castellammare di Stabia shipyard on 13 October. The demonstrations included technologies already in use, systems undergoing testing and solutions being developed for future operations. Bringing AI and robotics into shipbuilding The programme focuses on moving new technologies from testing into regular shipyard operations. One of its main areas is Physical AI, which allows intelligent systems to interact with machinery and their surroundings. Fincantieri is also developing collaborative robots to support workers during complex production tasks. Other technologies include digital twins, which create digital models of shipyard assets and processes, and smart supply chain systems designed to improve production planning and coordination. The company is also exploring additive manufacturing and automated industrial equipment. To support these developments, Fincantieri works with technology companies, startups and research partners. The aim is to adapt new solutions to shipbuilding requirements before introducing them across more facilities. Expanding technology across the shipyard network Fincantieri is now focusing on wider adoption of technologies that have already shown promising results. “The next frontier of industrial competitiveness is bringing artificial intelligence into the physical world, integrating it with robotics and the expertise embedded in our manufacturing operations,” said Pierroberto Folgiero, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director of Fincantieri. The company plans to continue testing new applications while expanding the use of existing systems. It also aims to strengthen cooperation between engineering, production and technology teams. Through BOOST², Fincantieri is seeking to make automation and digital technologies a regular part of its shipbuilding operations.

articles.title: Sea-Intelligence: Liner Networks Getting More Specialized
articles.summary: The global container shipping industry is undergoing a structural transformation, with shipping lines transitioning away from the highly homogenized networks of the past decade toward a landscape characterized by greater operational specialization. Prior to 2017, the deep‑sea network was heavily consolidated. To...
articles.body: The global container shipping industry is undergoing a structural transformation, with shipping lines transitioning away from the highly homogenized networks of the past decade toward a landscape characterized by greater operational specialization. Prior to 2017, the deep‑sea network was heavily consolidated. To maintain global market coverage, shipping lines relied extensively on dense Vessel Sharing Agreements (VSAs) to pool capacity. This operational strategy created a deeply homogenized market, wherein the same physical service was marketed under multiple brand names by different shipping lines, creating an illusion of choice for shippers. Recent years point to a stark divergence between the physical expansion of liner networks and the contraction of commercial offerings. While the underlying physical network has expanded from roughly 250 active deep‑sea services in 2012‑2013 to nearly 380 by late 2026, the number of shipping lines actively offering space across these services has steadily declined. This shifting dynamic is most clearly illustrated by Figure 1, which calculates the average density of vessel sharing in the market. Source: Sea-Intelligence.com, Sunday Spotlight, issue 786 During the peak of market homogenization in 2014‑2016, the average liner service was a highly shared asset. A single physical liner service was offered as a product by an average of 4.12 shipping lines. By August 2026, this multiplier has dropped to just 2.65, showing that shipping lines are demonstrably reducing their reliance on shared capacity and are instead increasingly choosing to shoulder more of the operational risk individually. Consequently, physical routing options are becoming increasingly distinct, signalling the return of true operational competition in the market.

articles.body: Charlie Cunnion Names as Massport New Port Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 15, 2026 © Massport The Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport) announced the appointment of Charlie Cunnion as Port Director. Cunnion brings over 25 years of leadership experience across global transportation, supply chain management, operations, organizational transformation, and strategic planning. Most recently, he served as Vice President of Supply Chain and Customer Service for CMPC Forest Products North America, where he led a business transformation focused on operational excellence, technology innovation, customer service, and culture change. Cunnion began his career at International Forest Products (IFP), where he rose to the position of Vice President of Global Transportation. While at IFP, he was responsible for 4.2m metric tons of annual freight, logistics service contracts across all modes of transportation and digitization of supply chain processes. In 2024, he joined the joint venture between IFP and CMPC SPA that became CMPC Forest Products North America, where he was the Vice President of Supply Chain Management and Customer Service. Cunnion helped design the new business plan and company framework, oversaw the implementation of a new customer-first operation and reduced supply chain costs by 21 percent. Cunnion is a graduate of Nichols College, where he received Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, Double Major in Economics and Finance. He also was an officer in the U.S Army, rising to the rank of Captain and receiving two Bronze Star Medals during deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. He serves on the board of the Foreign Commerce Club of Boston and the Sharon Cooperative & Nature School. He is also involved with industry associations such as the Northeast Association of Rail Shippers, the Coalition of New England Companies for Trade and the International Forest Products Transport Association. The Port of Boston generates $8.2 billion in annual economic impact and supports more than 66,000 jobs. Keeping the Port competitive to generate future economic growth and support job creation is an essential part of the Authority’s mission. As Port Director, Cunnion will lead Massport's Maritime Division. “Charlie is an expert in supply chain management, with decades of experience across all modes of cargo transportation,” said Massport CEO Rich Davey. “His leadership, experience and strategic perspective will be invaluable to the Port of Boston as we work to strengthen operations and continue a tradition of innovation and growth. I am thrilled to have him on my leadership team and look forward to seeing him build on the success of Conley Terminal and Flynn Cruiseport in his new role.” Conley Container Terminal enables more than 2,500 businesses throughout Massachusetts and New England to ship and receive products globally, including furniture and home goods, footwear, clothing, office supplies, wine and spirits, recycled fibers, sporting goods, seafood and more. In 2025, the terminal strengthened its reach with new international routes, welcomed the largest ships in its history, and moved over 1.7 million metric tons of cargo—underscoring its role in powering regional trade and economic growth. Flynn Cruiseport Boston continues to serve more passengers and cruise ships each year. With over 454,000 passengers and 149 ship calls in 2025, Flynn Cruiseport helped boost economic activity and tourism in the Commonwealth, generating $256 million annually in economic impact and creating over 3,000 jobs. Massport has committed over $100 million toward upgrades at Flynn Cruiseport, including expanding the waiting area with increased seating capacity and restrooms, streamlining the security check-in and installing a new escalator to improve passenger flow. As larger ships visit the region, the Cruiseport will be prepared for the future. Massport also announced a plan to bring ship-to-shore power to the Cruiseport by 2030. Nearly 80 percent of the ships that currently serve Boston can plug into shore power or use alternative low-carbon technology. When ships use shore power, they tap landside electricity for their power needs at berth including lights, pumps, communications, and refrigeration, instead of running diesel-fueled auxiliary on-board engines.

articles.title: The Markets Impacting the Revival of US Naval & Commercial Shipbuilding
articles.summary: The U.S. Maritime Industry is sifting through a nearly two-year decision process after Executive Order 14269 announcements of “Maritime Dominance” of April 9th 2025. Initially reported as the strongest federal support in decades, longer periods…
articles.body: The Markets Impacting the Revival of US Naval & Commercial Shipbuilding Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Robert Kunkel , Contributor Robert Kunkel, President of Alternative Marine Technologies... October 15, 2026 Copyright IanDewarPhotography/AdobeStock The U.S. Maritime Industry is sifting through a nearly two-year decision process after Executive Order 14269 announcements of “Maritime Dominance” of April 9th 2025. Initially reported as the strongest federal support in decades, longer periods of delays have also occurred as congress debates the Ships for America Act which has been passed from committee to committee in Congress. Legislation proposed to support American shipbuilding and the US flag commercial fleet and to date, has not reached the floor. Recently, the Maritime Administration advised the government effort is a different maritime revival. An understatement considering the Federal government’s first move was to issue a “Jones Act” waiver on March 17, 2026, allowing foreign vessels to trade in the coastal energy market. To be fair, the announcement was made through the Department of Homeland Security and reported without MarAd’s knowledge. The waiver disrupted U.S. flag coastal energy trading on all three coasts and has raised many unanswered questions on the direction the Administration is taking or for that matter who is making the decisions. The irony of the revival statement is the fact that the “Act” has long been described as the backbone of the country’s maritime industry. Considering the current global geopolitical events, the waiver decisions also question the claim of National Security, historically supported by Transcom and Military Sealift Command. Most would agree it could not be more important at this time. With issues continuing in the Straits of Hormuz, the waiver’s promise of gasoline price reduction did not occur during the first five months of foreign vessel trading. The energy costs continue to rise despite an extension put into place on August 13, 2026. Attempts to track the foreign flag cargo movements have been poor at best with estimates ranging from 200 to 400 voyages occurring during the two periods. Considering MarAd’s understanding that cargo is a part of this revival, it would be our opinion coastal movements is an important market that should be considered as a US “Maritime Dominance” priority. Certainly, with the fact that we have now invested over one and a half billion dollars in state maritime training vessels to recover the lack of seafaring labor. It is not only cargo; the success of a “market” is what drives commercial shipbuilding and investment. Simply put, the direction and success of commercial US shipbuilding is not only preference cargo. It is building at competitive costs to enter a market that employs American seafarers and provide the ability to renew an aging fleet. The lack of US shipyard subsidy is the problem and it is needed to meet that goal. We cannot compete commercially against foreign operating costs and capital of ship construction or labor. The original Ships For America Act legislation contains a shipbuilding incentives subsection 53801 interpreted to believe Congress and the Federal Government understands shipyard subsidy is required for commercial shipbuilding if we are to make any attempt to compete with any foreign shipyard. The description of the incentive allows a comparison of a US build cost to a foreign build of a coastal registered vessel not competing with current operators or looking to trade in an area where the specific vessel type is not available. The approval results in subsidy against the comparable US to foreign cost differential. Amtech has submitted a project to the Maritime Administrator with that objective. A US shipyard partner and a financial supporter are involved who have built the vessel type in foreign yards and a US yard to confirm the costs. Here is the problem. The foreign contracted cost is not a real number. The delivered foreign contract takes into account the shipbuilding subsidies provided by their governments whether Chinese, Korean, Japanese or European (the ship design has been built in more than several foreign countries). The US shipyard costs do not. In our opinion the project may open doors to understanding the US “cost to build” problem when competing against foreign yards. Our intent is to continue to support the industry as we have for decades. That said if the current administration is looking to reinvent the wheel, look to those who were around when the wheel was actually built. Many of the industry problems are repeated historical events which have not been corrected and if not addressed now will result in the revival failing again without accomplishing simple goals. An undated still image released on Oct. 6 from video taken by an Arabian Fox MAST-13 of an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy patrol speedboat in the Strait of Hormuz. Seven task forces falling under U.S. 5th Fleet integrated 12 different unmanned platforms with manned ships for “manned-unmanned teaming” operations tracking Iranian Navy and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy (IRGCN) ships and small boats over several days during routine patrols in and around the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Navy photo Begin by completely separating Naval and commercial ship construction. The successful Far East yards have been structured in this manner for decades. Owner/Operators build according to market supply and demand. Shipyards design and build according to their own markets and business models. Military and commercial ship construction are two different animals. Naval shipbuilding markets follow geopolitical events and we are drowning in those global events as we speak. Give the Department of War credit for understanding that Navy shipbuilding has changed. Drones, UAV, Autonomous surface, conventional submarines and Arctic requirements are the latest additions to our Destroyers, Nuclear Carriers and Submarines fleets. US shipbuilding defense capacity and government investment has already responded to these new problems and requirements. The US Navy was originally built to serve and protect the American coasts, our commercial ships and trade. The global shift in that operation occurred after World War II as the United States emerged as the world’s industrial and naval superpower. The only fleet left standing The 1944 Bretton Woods agreement established a postwar international financial system and the U.S. committed to a strategy guaranteeing a secure, free use of the oceans for all nations, including former adversaries. This created the maritime environment necessary for modern globalization. We were no longer tasked to defend or project power. The US Navy protected free trade. Free trade is now under attack. Circa 1979 the U.S. reestablished the post-WWII role by establishing the DoD Freedom of Navigation Program. The Navy regularly conducted freedom of navigation operations worldwide to challenge and ensure international sea lanes remained open under international law. As many debate the lack of Naval budget and government support during the post-cold war period, take a moment to realize what the actual threat was to commercial shipping and the US flag vessels that were operating internationally. We are being challenged to return to that role with the continued threat of a “ghost” fleet and free trade is again being defended with force. Nearly 10 years later, Operation Earnest Will (1987–1988) was developed during the tanker war of the Iran-Iraq conflict. Iranian forces utilized mines and speedboats to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. In response to the escalation, threatening over 20% of the world's oil supply, the U.S. Navy launched its largest convoy escort operation since WWII. We reflagged Kuwaiti oil tankers and actively escorted tonnage through the Gulf, while destroying Iranian gunboats and mining platforms to keep the Strait open. Apologies for not wanting to miss this opportunity to quote Yogi Berra as we compare the current Middle East situation as an example of history repeating itself. Its “Déjà vu all over again” We previously noted the dates the Executive orders and commerce reports were issued. The Straits were open and oil flowed. The Naval ship construction concerns at that time prepared for an Indo Pacific theater requiring both projecting military power and defending both ally and homeland. The latest Middle East conflict has now presented two fronts on a possible war footing. Ukraine and Russia have presented a third. Through more than several Federal Administrations, strategic Pentagon reports have advised the existing Naval fleet was not capable of supporting two fronts. Naval shipbuilding needs to be funded, take precedence, and utilize our shipyard capacity to build a war time labor force and deliver a fleet capable of reestablishing free trade and preserve National Security. Add the control of Greenland to the discussions or the Canadian Prime Minister stating in a September 2026 interview with the New York Times that his government examined the possibility of a U.S. military invasion of Canada, describing it as an "extreme tail risk", and ship construction takes on a entirely different discussion. Unfortunately, US commercial shipbuilding may have to take a back seat for the moment. Extreme geopolitical events effect trade. Commercial markets adjust to those changes and with that so do technical and operational requirements of ship types. Simple examples of the new interest in Venezuelan sources of methanol, the new routes of the Arctic requiring ice class tonnage, or the rebuilding of Ukraine & Cuba will take time to develop and significant risk analysis. The new interest in developing construction with allied shipyards under the “Finland” ice breaker concept or the “bridge” concept of Naval Auxiliary support vessels with new designs and efficiencies look to decrease that time. As commercial shipbuilders we have to meet a different cost standard and deliver according to an investment business plan to compete in a foreign market or for that matter support our military. Our long-term goal this time around is to make sure Yogi is not quoted again and let a new history develop. * As published in the October 2026 edition of Marine News.

The vessel subsequently sank, with all 21 crew members safely evacuated. The image has not been independently verified. U.S. Central Command says the United States and its regional partners control the Strait of Hormuz, citing more than 40 commercial ships moving through the waterway in the past 24 hours, even as maritime security officials warn that attacks on merchant vessels are increasing and the threat to shipping remains severe. The statement Thursday came as the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) released a new assessment documenting a series of attacks on commercial shipping, including the sinking of a containership, and warning that further strikes remain highly likely. “The United States and regional partners control the strait as commercial vessels continue to transit despite unwarranted IRGC aggression,” CENTCOM said in a statement rejecting three Iranian claims . But the military’s assertion of control comes against a markedly different picture of commercial shipping conditions. Traffic remains far below prewar levels, vessels continue to face attacks along established transit routes, and Iran is still attempting to influence how ships move through the strait. According to JMIC’s October 15 advisory , U.S.-facilitated traffic totaled 121 vessel transits between October 11 and 14, an average of approximately 30 ships per day. That compares with a historical average of roughly 138 daily transits in 2025, before the war. CENTCOM’s latest figure of more than 40 ships covers a different 24-hour period and may indicate an increase in traffic. Still, the four-day JMIC average represents only about 22% of the prewar benchmark. Independent commercial tracking continues to show substantially fewer transits than U.S. military-assisted figures. JMIC reported single-digit daily movements in its separate tracking data, although the two sources use different methodologies and do not measure the same categories of traffic. The distinction matters because while ships are continuing to pass through Hormuz, the volume of traffic remains a fraction of normal levels. JMIC maintained its threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE , warning that deliberate hostile action against commercial vessels remains highly likely. The latest advisory documented eight projectile attacks in the strait on October 11 and 13, involving four tankers and four containerships. A separate attack on the products tanker PETRO DOLPHIN near Sohar, Oman, left two crew members missing. The most serious recent incident involved the Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE , which was struck by a projectile on October 13 , caught fire and subsequently sank on October 14. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. CENTCOM rejected an Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claim that the vessel had struck a naval mine while traveling along an unauthorized route. “The civilian container ship M/V GFS Pride was hit by an IRGC projectile,” CENTCOM said, adding that the vessel sank while being towed to shore. The military also maintained that the strait’s primary shipping routes remain clear of mines. JMIC separately said there was no evidence supporting Iran’s claim that a mine caused the sinking. However, the advisory continued to warn mariners about potential mining activity within and around the established traffic separation scheme. It also warned of a continuing threat from IRGC surveillance, drone overflights, radio hailing and attempts to direct merchant ships toward the northern Iranian-controlled route. Vessels using the southern Omani corridor remain exposed to attacks, while those broadcasting their positions through the Automatic Identification System (AIS) face an elevated targeting risk, according to JMIC. The organization also cautioned mariners about floating containers and debris near the wreck of GFS PRIDE . The latest attacks are part of a broader escalation that began before October. JMIC now counts 149 confirmed vessel incidents across the region since March 1, including nine newly documented incidents in its latest reporting period. The International Maritime Organization separately lists 113 highlighted confirmed incidents and 24 seafarer fatalities as of October 14. The two organizations maintain different incident datasets and their totals are not directly comparable. Meanwhile, large numbers of commercial vessels remain at anchor throughout the region. JMIC reported approximately 180 vessels near Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, another 178 between Dubai, Jebel Ali and Ras Al Khaimah, and 74 around Musandam and Sohar as of October 15. The security situation is further complicated by the continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports. According to the latest figures cited by JMIC, U.S. forces had redirected 135 commercial vessels and disabled four during blockade enforcement operations as of October 10-11. Neutral shipping remains permitted to transit, although vessels can expect military hailing, monitoring and possible inspections. The latest JMIC advisory also warned that ships using either the northern Iranian-controlled route or the southern Omani corridor should expect continued security risks and reduced traffic. That leaves a significant gap between the military’s claim of control and the conditions facing commercial operators. U.S. forces are facilitating vessel movements through the strait, and commercial ships continue to transit. But attacks have continued despite the military presence, and shipping volumes remain well below their prewar levels. For shipowners, charterers and crews, the remaining question is whether the United States can provide enough security for normal commercial operations to resume, rather than simply keeping the waterway open to traffic willing to accept the risks. articles.title: Seven Sailors Missing After Chemical Tankers Struck Near Romania
articles.summary: Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.Romanian President…
articles.body: Seven Sailors Missing After Chemical Tankers Struck Near Romania Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 15, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zerophoto Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones but declined to say whether Russia was responsible, while a NATO military source said the drones came from Russia. "The drones that caused the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin," the NATO source said. The two vessels were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina canal leading into the Danube River, a major export route used by Ukraine as Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukraine's Black Sea ports. One was inside Romanian territorial waters and the other just outside. The missing crew were among 12 sailors aboard the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader, which was hit 13 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, one mile outside Romanian waters. Five crew members were rescued, Romanian officials said. The second vessel, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, caught fire after being struck 8-10 miles southeast of Sulina inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday. All crew were safe. The attacks are the latest in a series of strikes on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea. At least five other cargo vessels have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring NATO member Bulgaria over the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported missing or dead. Those attacks occurred outside NATO territorial waters. "The situation in the Black Sea is serious," Romania's Dan said. "Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured, and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake." SEARCH FOR MISSING SAILORS The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as well as two ships with medical staff on board. "At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," it said in a statement. NATO said in a statement it was in contact with Romanian officials. It added two other vessels had been targeted in the Black Sea overnight, Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier Sea Destiny inside Romanian waters and Tanzanian-flagged tanker Dania J, moored in the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail. It did not mention casualties. "NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed," NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said after meeting Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Thursday. ATTACKS ON BLACK SEA SHIPPING Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since the start of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The escalating attacks on Black Sea shipping have heightened concerns over grain exports from the region. Russian attacks on Ukraine's own Black Sea ports have forced Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. Ukraine, for its part, has targeted Russian vessels near the mouth of the Don River in the Azov Sea. Bulgaria's Radev said EU leaders would discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. "We're looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told a security conference in Warsaw earlier this week. "It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence." articles.summary: The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen.

REUTERS/Khaled Abdullah DUBAI, Oct 15 (Reuters) – The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen. By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions, they aim to pressure Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to both meet Houthi demands in Yemen and persuade US President Donald Trump to ease the US blockade choking Iran’s economy, according to Saudi, Iranian and regional sources. The campaign reflects a calculation by Iran and the Houthis that Saudi Arabia’s prosperity, investment ambitions and exposure to disruption make it a vulnerable pressure point in a confrontation stretching from the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf to Bab el-Mandeb in the Red Sea. Iran, under mounting economic and military pressure following the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, is seeking to raise the cost of Washington’s strategy by targeting its regional partners, said Michael Knights of strategic advisory Horizon Engage. “The Iranians are in a chokehold,” he said. Unable to force Washington to change course directly, Tehran and the Houthis are “hammering Saudi Arabia, they’re hammering the weak point,” he added, exploiting the kingdom’s economic vulnerability and desire for stability. The Houthis have a direct interest in easing the US blockade on Iran, their principal regional backer. A relaxation of pressure on Tehran would likely strengthen its ability to sustain the political, financial and military support and flow of weapons and cash on which the US says the movement depends. But the Houthis also have their own demands, said two Saudi sources and three regional sources familiar with Saudi thinking: an end to Saudi military operations and restrictions on Yemeni ports and airports, regular flights to Iran, restored salary payments, war compensation and an end to Riyadh’s support for Yemen’s recognized government. Their terms would consolidate Houthi rule over much of Yemen. A senior Iranian official said the Houthi attacks were part of a broader strategy by Iran and its allies to reshape the regional balance of power by targeting energy infrastructure and key shipping routes. He said Riyadh could not rely on US protection and must instead pursue negotiations, adding that Houthi attacks would continue unless Saudi restrictions were lifted. The strategy, however, leaves MbS facing a dilemma, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking say. Escalation risks a wider war that could undermine his transformation agenda, but concessions risk strengthening a movement that has challenged Saudi power for years. And the longer the conflict drags on, the greater the threat to Saudi security, investor confidence and Vision 2030. The Saudi government media office, Iran’s foreign ministry and a Houthi spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam denied that the group was acting at Iran’s behest, saying its demands were centered on longstanding humanitarian issues relating to Saudi Arabia, and included lifting restrictions on Yemeni ports, airports, easing economic restrictions, and paying civil servants’ salaries from Yemen’s own resources. “Our humanitarian demands have nothing to do with Iran or anyone else,” he said. FLAGSHIP CONFERENCES DISRUPTED Saudi Arabia has faced a widening wave of Houthi attacks over the past week, including deadly strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and a strike on Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil exporter and a backbone of the economy, which sparked a fire that spread across several floors. The attacks have disrupted Riyadh’s flagship oil conference, prompting top oil executives to withdraw, and forced organizers to offer remote participation at the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual global investment forum. The Houthis have a record of striking deep inside the kingdom, including in 2019, when attacks on Aramco facilities temporarily disrupted about 5% of global oil supply. That was after Riyadh intervened in Yemen in 2015 following the Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate before a 2022 ceasefire. However, Saudi leaders now see military pressure as their only viable option, said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center. “They reached a point of NO negotiations,” he said. “They have no other choice except military action.” The Houthis increasingly see themselves as negotiating from strength, seeking recognition of their authority in Sanaa and an easing of restrictions on Yemen, said Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East analyst at the London School of Economics. “What the Houthis are asking now is a victor’s peace,” he said. The United States has shown little appetite for another sustained campaign against the Houthis since bombing them last year over attacks on shipping in the Red Sea then agreeing a ceasefire, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking said. Washington’s reluctance leaves Riyadh facing a conflict in which military pressure alone may not deliver a decisive outcome. SAUDIS HAVE MORE TO LOSE At the start of the Houthi campaign, MbS asked Trump for help to fight the Houthis, but Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing. Trump later said he was considering possible action against the Houthis, while appearing to defer any response until after the US midterm elections. The US State Department referred to previous remarks by Trump and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. With drones and missiles exposing vulnerabilities in Saudi defenses, analysts warn the conflict risks becoming a war of attrition in which the Houthis believe time and geography favor them. Former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the group’s advantage lies not only in its position near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint but also in the asymmetry of what is at stake. “Saudi infrastructure is much more valuable than Houthi infrastructure,” he said. “They have so much less to lose than the Saudis.” Yemen analyst Farea al-Muslimi said the Houthis’ campaign against Riyadh is a bid to assert regional primacy, risking a far broader conflict across the Arabian Peninsula. At the heart of the crisis, he says, is the unraveling of a 2023 Saudi-backed peace roadmap that offered the Houthis a path to political legitimacy and reconstruction funding. Under the roadmap, Riyadh was set to help fund public sector salaries and rebuilding. The Red Sea conflict has derailed that process as the Houthis deepen their alignment with Iran. “We’re heading towards the worst outcome imaginable,” al-Muslimi said. “A war worse than 2015. This time it will be bloodier, and Saudi Arabia will enter it with fewer allies.” He said no successful campaign against the Houthis was possible without Gulf unity, mainly between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. “The Houthis are not a threat to Saudi Arabia alone,” he said. “They threaten the entire Gulf and the wider region. This is not simply a Saudi war. It is a Gulf war.” (Additional reporting by Parisa Hafezi in Dubai, Ahmed Tolba in Cairo and Mohammed Ghobari; Writing by Samia Nakhoul; Editing by Aidan Lewis) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. (U.S. Navy photo) Five people have been arrested in Norway as part of an international investigation into suspected fraud and bribery involving a company providing port services to NATO warships. The arrests were carried out Wednesday, October 14, alongside coordinated searches in Romania and Germany, according to Eurojust , the European Union’s agency for criminal justice cooperation. Investigators suspect the company and its subcontractors submitted fraudulent invoices to the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) for husbandry services provided to military vessels during port calls in northwestern Europe. Husbandry services cover essential shoreside support for ships and their crews during port visits. Authorities estimate the alleged scheme has cost NATO member countries more than €1 million, although the full extent of the suspected fraud remains under investigation. The investigation also includes allegations that the company used an intermediary to bribe foreign public officials in exchange for favorable treatment in its contractual dealings with the NSPA. The NSPA, NATO’s primary logistics and procurement agency, identified the suspicious invoices and subsequently worked with investigators to provide evidence and information. Wednesday’s coordinated operation resulted in five arrests in Norway, where authorities also searched residential and business properties. In Romania, investigators searched company premises and several homes, while German authorities searched two businesses and a residence. The cross-border investigation began receiving support from Eurojust in April 2025. A joint investigation team was established three months later, bringing together authorities from Norway, Romania and the United Kingdom to share evidence and coordinate their work. German authorities also participated in the latest operation, with searches conducted in Hamburg under a European Investigation Order. Authorities involved include Norway’s economic crime agency Økokrim, Romania’s National Anticorruption Directorate, the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service and Ministry of Defence Police, and prosecutors and police in Hamburg. Eurojust did not identify the company or the individuals arrested and said it could not provide further details while the investigation continues. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo HOUSTON/LOS ANGELES, Oct 15 (Reuters) – When the oil supertanker Esteem Explorer sails from the United States to Japan in late November, loaded with about 2 million barrels of crude, the journey will cost $81 million. The same journey would have cost $9.1 million last year, on average. The shipping cost translates into $40.50 per barrel, about nine times last year’s rate. While oil’s soaring selling price worries consumers, the Esteem Explorer’s expensive voyage illustrates how transport costs are further inflating the price. Refiners process oil into fuel to move food, retail goods and construction materials, and rising costs are stoking inflation in countries that depend on imports. Every $10-per-barrel increase in shipping costs adds about 23 cents per gallon to gasoline, said Kenneth Medlock, a fellow in energy and resource economics at the Houston-based Baker Institute for Public Policy. On that basis, the Esteem Explorer’s shipping cost works out to at least 80 cents more per gallon of gasoline than last year, according to Reuters calculations. “It’s sort of like a slow-moving train. It doesn’t all happen instantly … but the longer this drags on, the more sticky it becomes, which means you get more of a sustained impact at the grocery store, in the convenience store, at the mall,” Medlock said. “Everything gets more expensive because that’s how we move stuff around.” Freight rates account for more than 40% of the price of US oil, based on Wednesday’s price around $95 per barrel, compared with 7% on average in 2025, according to LSEG shipping and oil price data. Countries reliant on imports — including India, the Philippines and Indonesia — bear the brunt of the soaring costs, Medlock said. Record oil tanker rates are already squeezing Asian refiners’ profits, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday. Refiners process oil into gasoline for cars, diesel for semi-trucks and farm equipment, and jet fuel for airplanes. Attacks on ships related to the US-Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war have boosted freight and insurance rates. Rates to move oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea in the Middle East to Asia surged to a record high around $34 per barrel this week, as shippers price in a risk premium for attacks on vessels. Fearing attack, ships are also sailing longer routes than before, tying up tankers longer. Shippers moving Saudi oil are using more vessels than before — transferring oil ship to ship — to reduce the risks for individual ships after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline increased exports via the Strait of Hormuz. That strategy has reduced ship availability, raising costs and increasing the time cargoes are on the water. The resulting shortage of very large crude carriers such as the Esteem Explorer has lifted prices for smaller vessels. Freight rates have quadrupled since the Iran war began in February for Suezmax ships, which can carry up to 1 million barrels of oil, for a route between the US Gulf Coast and Asia, and for Aframaxes, which carry up to 750,000 barrels, on the US Gulf Coast to Europe route, according to Signal Ocean. While some shippers contract vessels for three to five years, many of them charter ships on the spot market about a month prior to loading. The long-term contracts, in which shippers and vessel owners lock in prices, could prove to be bargains for the shippers if prices rise further. Oil market upheaval has provided a windfall for tanker owners. They have recently earned as much as $1.3 million per ship per day for a round trip from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz to Asia, said Georgios Sakellariou, a Signal Ocean freight analyst. That compared with earnings of $55,000 per ship per day on average in 2025. “If you’d have told me six weeks ago that we were seeing a million dollars per day, I wouldn’t have believed you,” said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior analyst at maritime intelligence firm Windward. This year may be the most profitable ever, said a person at a company that owns and operates tankers primarily in the Americas. “Our expectation is that as long as there is more crude oil demand than supply, tanker rates will remain strong. However, as soon as the crude oil market loosens, tanker rates will come off the boil quickly,” said Erik Broekhuizen, head of tanker research and consulting at ship broker Poten & Partners. Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS (Bloomberg) — Shipowners are facing an increasingly fragmented fuel market as disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict raise concerns about the availability and quality of supply. Ships can’t always refuel at familiar ports if they’re forced on longer journeys around Africa and diverted to the Atlantic Basin to avoid escalating hostilities near the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. That’s turned other locations into so-called bunkering hubs and driven up fuel prices. “No one can treat bunkering as a routine, last-minute decision anymore,” said Frederik Guttormsen, Asia Pacific president at Stolt-Nielsen Ltd., an operator of 167 tankers that transport chemicals worldwide. “We’re securing fuel earlier and tracking availability and lead times at key ports because the risk is now as much about prompt supply as about price.” Middle East oil flows are coming under renewed strain from recent attacks in the region, including on vessels transiting Hormuz. The disruptions are pushing oil and bunker prices higher, Guttormsen said. He made the comments on the sidelines of a shipping conference in Singapore known as Sibcon. Singapore, the world’s biggest ship-refueling hub, continues to see growth, while vessels are tending to avoid Fujairah on the east coast of the United Arab Emirates, south of Hormuz. Other locations seeing higher bunkering demand since the US-Iran war include Port Louis in Mauritius, South Africa, West Africa, Brazil, Sri Lanka and Pakistan, according to participants at Sibcon. Bunkering at less familiar ports may expose shipowners to smaller or less reputable sellers, as well as wider price disparities between locations. Differences can reflect factors including fuel sourcing, access to on-spec feedstock and the availability of support services needed to ensure quality and compliance. “In this market, procurement needs to be much more structured,” said Kenneth Dam, executive director and global head of bunkering at TFG Marine, a major trader and supplier of ship fuels. Vessels are also refueling more frequently and taking smaller volumes at each stop to avoid locking in too much fuel at a particular price and port, he said. Disruptions are also becoming more frequent, leading to vessel diversions that are shifting fuel demand to other locations, said Peter Grünwaldt, head of bunkering at tanker owner Hafnia Ltd. and co-chief executive officer of bunker trader Seascale Energy. “We’re making sure we have fuel available at these ports,” he said. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. The vessel is being held as part of a UK-led investigation into alleged sanctions violations and shadow fleet activity. Royal Navy Photo Britain has expanded its sanctions against Russia’s oil industry, targeting two more energy companies, a dozen shadow-fleet tankers and financial networks used to move money around Western restrictions. The measures, announced October 8 as part of a package of 38 sanctions targets, bring more than 90% of Russia’s oil production capacity under UK sanctions, according to the British government. The latest action also targets companies supplying equipment used in Russia’s missile and drone programs. The sanctions come as London and Washington appear to be moving in different directions on Russian oil. The Trump administration is considering easing restrictions on sanctioned tankers in an effort to reduce record-high freight rates, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Britain is urging its allies to tighten restrictions on the shipping services supporting Russia’s oil trade. At the center of the latest UK package are Russian oil companies Zarubezhneft and INK Capital. Their addition follows earlier sanctions against Russia’s largest oil producers, including Rosneft and Lukoil. British officials say the broader coverage is intended not only to restrict Russian oil revenues but also to make it harder for sanctioned producers to sell crude through companies that have not yet been blacklisted. The government’s claim that sanctions now cover more than 90% of Russian oil production capacity does not mean an equivalent share of production has stopped. Russian oil continues to reach international markets through trading and shipping networks that have adapted to Western restrictions. The package also includes 12 shadow-fleet tankers previously reported by gCaptain , bringing Britain’s total number of sanctioned shadow-fleet oil tankers to more than 600. Among the newly listed vessels is the 22-year-old product tanker Dakar , which was making a late-season voyage along Russia’s Northern Sea Route. The designation comes amid growing use of the Arctic shipping corridor by older and sanctioned vessels carrying Russian energy exports to Asian markets. Britain is also targeting the financial infrastructure behind Russia’s sanctions evasion efforts. The package includes three cryptocurrency exchanges, two payment platforms and an individual linked to financial transactions, with several targets connected to Kyrgyzstan. Two of the targeted platforms have processed transactions involving the Kremlin-backed A7 financial network, according to the UK Foreign Office. The network claimed to have moved more than $90 billion last year, an amount Britain said was equivalent to roughly half of Russia’s annual military spending. Another 17 individuals and entities were sanctioned for their involvement in supplying goods that Western governments consider important to Russia’s military production. These include importers of machine tools, electronics and other components used to manufacture ballistic missiles and drones. The UK said some suppliers have used third countries to conceal trade with Russia, highlighting the difficulty of restricting goods that can move through multiple intermediaries before reaching Russian manufacturers. The widening sanctions campaign comes at a particularly difficult time for the global tanker market. Freight rates have surged as conflict in the Middle East disrupts shipping and raises demand for available vessels. Washington is now weighing whether to allow previously sanctioned tankers to carry oil and petroleum products that are not themselves subject to U.S. sanctions. Such a move would require companies to obtain authorization from the U.S. Treasury Department, according to Reuters. The U.S. Department of Energy has said any relief would not help Russia transport its oil. However, European and British restrictions would continue to apply independently, potentially limiting the ability of those vessels to obtain insurance and other shipping services. Britain’s finance minister, John Healey, on Thursday called for tougher international restrictions on maritime services supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, underscoring the growing difference between the two countries’ approaches. The discussions follow President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily lift restrictions on Russian diesel , another measure aimed at easing pressure on global energy markets. For shipping companies, the different approaches create an increasingly complicated sanctions environment. Even if Washington relaxes restrictions on some tankers, vessels and their commercial partners could remain subject to British and European measures. Department of War photo By Timothy Gardner and Jarrett Renshaw WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) – The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday. The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump’s fellow Republicans in the US Senate. Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine. The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing “legal oil” to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures. The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group. Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available. Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said. The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy. But Trump’s push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels. The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment. High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7. RECORD HIGHS Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to ?seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East. Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is “unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months,” it said in the note. Easing the restrictions “could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs,” in the waterway between Iran and Oman. Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said. October 15, 2026 Image courtesy Shipnext Belgium-based Shipnext has introduced business networking capabilities to its digital shipping marketplace, enabling charterers, brokers, carriers and cargo owners to communicate and exchange freight information within a single platform. Launched October 16, 2026, the new functionality integrates professional networking with Shipnext's existing freight-matching, cargo and fleet-positioning tools, aiming to reduce the industry's reliance on email for exchanging cargo availability, vessel schedules and freight information. The platform now supports open and closed group chats, allowing shipping professionals to establish business connections, share market intelligence and discuss cargo and vessel availability within dedicated industry communities. According to Shipnext, more than 1,000 chartering professionals have already joined its networking environment. The company argues that traditional email-based communication creates inefficiencies in freight markets, where cargo requirements, vessel positions and schedules are frequently exchanged through fragmented correspondence. Shipnext's approach draws comparisons to the traditional Baltic Exchange trading model, bringing shipping professionals together in a centralized digital marketplace. Earlier in 2026, Shipnext integrated CMA CGM's bookable freight services and schedules, expanding its coverage across containerized shipping alongside dry bulk, wet bulk, breakbulk and oversized cargo. By combining freight transactions, market data and professional communication, Shipnext aims to streamline commercial shipping operations while providing a dedicated networking environment for the global maritime trading community. articles.summary: Lloyd’s Register (LR) has published new Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices highlighting the growing complexity of ship retrofit projects.As regulatory and commercial pressures increase through measures such as FuelEU Maritime…
articles.body: LR Publishes Alternative Fuel Retrofit Guidelines Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 15, 2026 The bow of a large cargo ship in dry dock. Image by jaslagman0 from Pixabay Lloyd’s Register (LR) has published new Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices highlighting the growing complexity of ship retrofit projects. As regulatory and commercial pressures increase through measures such as FuelEU Maritime, the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction ambitions, retrofitting existing vessels is becoming an increasingly important pathway for owners seeking to improve efficiency, reduce emissions and extend asset life. However, the challenge is no longer simply selecting a single fuel or technology. Retrofit projects have become increasingly complex, requiring careful consideration of fuel storage, engine compatibility, safety systems, crew training, statutory approvals, vessel design and long-term operational impacts. To help the industry navigate these challenges, LR’s new publication brings together alternative fuels and energy-saving devices within a single retrofit framework. It covers the practical considerations associated with converting vessels to LNG, methanol, ethanol, ammonia, hydrogen and LPG, alongside the installation of wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) and air lubrication systems (ALS). A central theme is that many retrofit decisions must be made much earlier in the process than owners may expect. Factors such as engine conversion capability, available onboard space, tank location, fuel-system integration and project execution can have a major influence on project costs, timelines and operational outcomes. The guidance emphasizes the importance of early collaboration between owners, shipyards, equipment manufacturers, flag administrations and classification societies to avoid delays and reduce project risk. The publication also highlights growing opportunities for energy-saving technologies. Wind-assisted propulsion systems, for example, can benefit from incentives under FuelEU Maritime through a reward factor designed to recognize their contribution to lowering greenhouse gas intensity At the same time, the guidance notes reflect growing industry recognition that retrofit projects must address both technical and human factors. Extensive crew training, revised operating procedures, updated safety management systems and new risk assessments are identified as essential elements of successful deployment, particularly for fuels such as ammonia and hydrogen, which introduce new safety considerations The Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices is available from LR’s Retrofit Research program: Ship Retrofitting | Retrofit Research Programme | LR

articles.body: Marine Energy October 15, 2026 · 20 hours ago Minesto reports 'record' 48-hour service intervention on its tidal power plant NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Minesto Minesto has performed a service intervention on its Dragon 4 tidal power plant in record time, carrying out the recovery, inspection, and redeployment offshore process in 48 hours, the Swedish ocean energy developer reported today, October 15. Minesto revealed that, after years of improving the process, it had achieved its fastest turnaround to date, with a complete service intervention of a Dragon 4 power plant performed within 48 hours in Vestmannasund, Faroe Islands. The intervention included recovery, extraction of the nacelle for inspection of the upgraded generator following its first ten weeks of operation, maintenance activities, reassembly, quality and functional checks, and redeployment offshore. The work was carried out during a low-production tidal period. Minesto "The ability to complete a full service operation and return the system to power production in only 48 hours demonstrates a key competitive advantage of our technology," said Martin Edlund , Minesto's CEO. "High performance is important, but equally important is the ability to maintain the system cost efficiently. Notably, our method does not rely on sophisticated and expensive infrastructure, making it suitable for remote locations and areas of the world without port infrastructure and access to advanced marine engineering capabilities." Minesto notes that the central feature of the concept is the ability to swap subsystems, such as the nacelle, during short intervention campaigns. By using spare modules, more extensive inspections, maintenance activities and upgrades can be performed onshore without impact on availability and energy yield. This capability becomes increasingly valuable as we move towards larger commercial deployments and multi-unit installations," said Bernt Erik Westre , CTO of Minesto.
